A.explanation: Taking moments about the pivot gives $W \times 1.0 = 50 \times 0.5$, so $W = 25 \text{ N}$.

B.explanation: This assumes the 50 N beam weight balances $W$ with equal lever arms, ignoring that the beam centre is only $0.5 \text{ m}$ from the pivot.

C.explanation: This is too large and would give a much larger anticlockwise moment about the pivot than the clockwise moment from the 50 N weight.

D.explanation: This would require the beam weight to act at $2.0 \text{ m}$ from the pivot, whereas the centre of the uniform 3.0 m beam is much closer to the pivot.

hints: Notice the pivot is $1.0 \text{ m}$ from P, but the uniform $3.0 \text{ m}$ beam has its $50 \text{ N}$ weight acting at its midpoint, $1.5 \text{ m}$ from P.
Compare perpendicular distances from the pivot: $W$ acts $1.0 \text{ m}$ to the left while the beam weight acts $0.5 \text{ m}$ to the right.
Set clockwise moment equal to anticlockwise moment about the pivot: $W \times 1.0 = 50 \times 0.5$ and solve for $W$.
walkthrough: The beam is uniform, so its $50 \text{ N}$ weight acts at its centre, $1.5 \text{ m}$ from end P.
The pivot is $1.0 \text{ m}$ from P, so the distance of the beam weight from the pivot is $1.5 - 1.0 = 0.5 \text{ m}$ to the right.
The load $W$ at P is $1.0 \text{ m}$ to the left of the pivot.
For equilibrium the sum of moments about the pivot is zero, so anticlockwise moment equals clockwise moment: $W \times 1.0 = 50 \times 0.5$.
Hence $W = 25 \text{ N}$. This is option A.
